{{Short description|Theorem in Optimal Transport}}

In [[Transportation theory (mathematics)|optimal transport]], a branch of mathematics, polar factorization of vector fields is a basic result due to Brenier (1987),<ref name="brenier">{{cite journal |last1=Brenier |first1=Yann |title=Polar factorization and monotone rearrangement of vector‐valued functions |journal=Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics |date=1991 |volume=44 |issue=4 |pages=375–417 |doi=10.1002/cpa.3160440402 |url=http://www.math.toronto.edu/~mccann/assignments/477/Brenier91.pdf |access-date=16 April 2021}}</ref> with antecedents of Knott-Smith (1984)<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Knott |first1=M. |last2=Smith |first2=C. S. |title=On the optimal mapping of distributions |journal=Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications |date=1984 |volume=43 |pages=39–49 |doi=10.1007/BF00934745 |s2cid=120208956 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00934745 |access-date=16 April 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and Rachev (1985),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rachev |first1=Svetlozar T. |title=The Monge–Kantorovich mass transference problem and its stochastic applications |journal=Theory of Probability & Its Applications |date=1985 |volume=29 |issue=4 |pages=647–676 |doi=10.1137/1129093 |url=https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~saito/data/emd/rachev.pdf |access-date=16 April 2021}}</ref> that generalizes many existing results among which are the [[polar decomposition]] of real matrices, and the rearrangement of real-valued functions.

==The theorem==
'' '''Notation.''' ''Denote <math>\xi_\# \mu</math> the [[Pushforward measure|image measure]] of <math>\mu</math> through the [[Map (mathematics)|map]] <math>\xi</math>.

'' '''Definition: Measure preserving map.''' '' Let <math>(X,\mu)</math> and <math>(Y,\nu)</math> be some [[probability spaces]] and <math>\sigma :X \rightarrow Y</math> a measurable map. Then, <math>\sigma</math> is said to be measure preserving iff <math>\sigma_{\#}\mu = \nu</math>, where <math>\#</math> is the [[pushforward measure]]. Spelled out: for every <math>\nu</math>-measurable subset <math>\Omega</math> of <math>Y</math>, <math>\sigma^{-1}(\Omega)</math> is <math>\mu</math>-measurable, and <math>\mu(\sigma^{-1}(\Omega))=\nu(\Omega )</math>. The latter is equivalent to: 
:<math> \int_{X}(f\circ \sigma)(x) \mu(dx) =\int_X (\sigma^*f)(x) \mu(dx) =\int_Y f(y) (\sigma_{\#}\mu)(dy) = \int_{Y}f(y) \nu(dy)</math>
where <math>f</math> is <math>\nu</math>-integrable and <math> f\circ \sigma </math> is <math>\mu</math>-integrable.

'' '''Theorem.''' '' Consider a map <math>\xi :\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d}</math> where <math>\Omega</math> is a convex subset of <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>, and <math>\mu</math> a measure on <math>\Omega</math> which is absolutely continuous. Assume that <math>\xi_{\#}\mu</math> is absolutely continuous. Then there is a [[convex function]] <math>\varphi :\Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> and a map <math>\sigma :\Omega \rightarrow \Omega</math> preserving <math>\mu</math> such that

<math> \xi =\left( \nabla \varphi \right) \circ \sigma </math>

In addition, <math>\nabla \varphi</math> and <math>\sigma</math> are uniquely defined almost everywhere.<ref name="brenier" /><ref name="Santambrogio">{{cite book |last1=Santambrogio |first1=Filippo |title=Optimal transport for applied mathematicians |date=2015 |publisher=Birkäuser |location=New York |citeseerx=10.1.1.726.35 }}</ref>

==Applications and connections==
===Dimension 1===
In dimension 1, and when <math>\mu</math> is the [[Lebesgue measure]] over the unit interval, the result specializes to Ryff's theorem.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ryff |first1=John V. |title=Orbits of L1-Functions Under Doubly Stochastic Transformation |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |date=1965 |volume=117 |pages=92–100 |doi=10.2307/1994198 |jstor=1994198 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1994198 |access-date=16 April 2021|url-access=subscription }}</ref> When <math>d=1</math> and <math>\mu</math> is the [[continuous uniform distribution|uniform distribution]] over <math>\left[0,1\right]</math>, the polar decomposition boils down to

<math> \xi \left( t\right) =F_{X}^{-1}\left( \sigma \left( t\right) \right) </math>

where <math>F_{X}</math> is cumulative distribution function of the random variable <math>\xi \left( U\right)</math> and <math>U</math> has a uniform distribution over <math>\left[ 0,1\right]</math>. <math>F_{X}</math> is assumed to be continuous, and <math>\sigma \left( t\right)=F_{X}\left( \xi \left( t\right) \right)</math> preserves the Lebesgue measure on <math>\left[ 0,1\right]</math>.

===Polar decomposition of matrices===
When <math>\xi</math> is a linear map and <math>\mu</math> is the Gaussian [[normal distribution]], the result coincides with the [[Polar decomposition|polar decomposition of matrices]]. Assuming <math>\xi \left( x\right) =Mx</math> where <math>M</math> is an invertible <math>d\times d</math> matrix and considering <math>\mu</math> the <math>\mathcal{N}\left( 0,I_{d}\right)</math> probability measure, the polar decomposition boils down to

<math>
M=SO
</math>

where <math>S</math> is a [[Symmetric matrix|symmetric]] [[Definite matrix|positive definite]] matrix, and <math>O</math> an [[orthogonal matrix]]. The connection with the polar factorization is <math>\varphi \left(x\right) =x^{\top }Sx/2</math> which is convex, and <math>\sigma \left( x\right) =Ox</math> which preserves the <math>\mathcal{N}\left( 0,I_{d}\right)</math> measure.

===Helmholtz decomposition===
The results also allow to recover [[Helmholtz decomposition]]. Letting <math>x\rightarrow V\left( x\right)</math> be a smooth [[vector field]] it can then be written in a unique way as

<math>
V=w+\nabla p
</math>

where <math>p</math> is a smooth real function defined on <math>\Omega</math>, unique up to an additive constant, and <math>w</math> is a smooth divergence free vector field, parallel to the boundary of <math>\Omega</math>.

The connection can be seen by assuming <math>\mu </math> is the Lebesgue measure on a compact set <math>\Omega \subset R^{n}</math> and by writing <math>\xi</math> as a perturbation of the [[identity map]]

<math>
\xi _{\epsilon }(x)=x+\epsilon V(x)
</math>

where <math>\epsilon</math> is small. The polar decomposition of <math>\xi _{\epsilon }</math> is given by <math>\xi _{\epsilon }=(\nabla \varphi_{\epsilon })\circ \sigma_{\epsilon }</math>. Then, for any test function <math>f:R^{n}\rightarrow R</math> the following holds:

<math>
\int_{\Omega }f(x+\epsilon V(x))dx=\int_{\Omega }f((\nabla \varphi
_{\epsilon })\circ \sigma _{\epsilon }\left( x\right) )dx=\int_{\Omega
}f(\nabla \varphi _{\epsilon }\left( x\right) )dx
</math>

where the fact that <math>\sigma _{\epsilon }</math> was preserving the Lebesgue measure was used in the second equality.

In fact, as <math>\textstyle \varphi _{0}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\Vert x\Vert ^{2}</math>, one can expand <math>\textstyle \varphi _{\epsilon }(x)=\frac{1}{2}\Vert x\Vert ^{2}+\epsilon p(x)+O(\epsilon ^{2})</math>, and therefore <math>\textstyle \nabla \varphi_{\epsilon }\left( x\right) =x+\epsilon \nabla p(x)+O(\epsilon ^{2})</math>. As a result, <math>\textstyle \int_{\Omega }\left( V(x)-\nabla p(x)\right) \nabla f(x))dx</math> for any smooth function <math>f</math>, which implies that <math>w\left( x\right) =V(x)-\nabla p(x)</math> is divergence-free.<ref name="brenier" /><ref name="Villani">{{cite book |last1=Villani |first1=Cédric |title=Topics in optimal transportation |date=2003 |publisher=American Mathematical Society}}</ref>
